The Sex Class Cannot Be Opted Into: A Radical Feminist Case for Female-Only Spaces

For over a century, feminism was the political movement of a definable class of people: women. That class was never constituted by dresses, hormones, mannerisms, or inner feelings. It was—and is—constituted by the material reality of the female body and the oppression visited upon that body from birth. What a Woman Is

Sex is not a spectrum, a feeling, or a social performance. It is a reproductive classification, observed in every human who has ever existed: females are the sex whose bodies are organized around the production of large gametes (ova); males are the sex organized around the production of small gametes (sperm). This binary is fixed at conception, expressed in every nucleated cell of the body, and unalterable by any medical intervention. No human being has ever changed sex. Cross-sex hormones and surgery can reshape secondary characteristics—breast tissue, fat distribution, genital appearance—but they cannot transform a male body into a female one, cannot produce ovaries or a uterus, cannot rewrite a development pathway that ran through male puberty.

Simone de Beauvoir wrote that one is not born, but rather becomes, a woman. Radical feminists have always understood her correctly: the female is born; the subordinate social role called "femininity" is imposed upon her. Gender, in the radical feminist analysis, is not an identity to be celebrated but a hierarchy to be abolished—the elaborate system of behaviors, expectations, and constraints that keeps the female sex subordinate to the male one. A transgender woman is a male who adopts the signifiers of that imposed hierarchy. However deeply felt that identification may be, an inner conviction cannot rewrite chromosomes, and the costumes of oppression worn willingly by males do not cease to be the costumes of oppression.

Women's rights are sex-based rights, and they exist because sex-based oppression exists. Sex-selective abortion, female genital mutilation, child marriage, reproductive coercion, maternal mortality, menstruation stigma, pregnancy discrimination—none of these atrocities pause to inquire how the victim identifies. Girls are valued less, fed less, educated less, and married off because of the bodies they are born into, not the identities they profess. The law protects "women" as a category precisely because of what female bodies are and what is systematically done to them.

If "woman" is redefined to mean "anyone who declares himself a woman," the category collapses as a matter of logic and law. A class defined purely by self-declaration cannot be measured, counted, or defended. We are already seeing the consequences: violent crimes and rapes committed by males recorded in official statistics as committed by "women," distorting the data on which policy depends; all-female shortlists, prizes, and scholarships opened to males; the very word "woman" displaced in medical language by degrading circumlocutions—"birthing people," "menstruators"—that erase the class while the male class is never renamed. Notably, when this question reached Britain's highest court, the UK Supreme Court held unanimously in 2025 that "sex" in the Equality Act means biological sex. Safety: The Central, Non-Negotiable Fact

Male violence is the central fact of female existence. Men commit the overwhelming majority of violent crime and roughly 98 percent of sexual offenses. Every woman alive has been shaped by this reality—the keys clutched between fingers, the public toilet visited in pairs, the vigilance in spaces of undress. This is not prejudice; it is pattern recognition learned from lived experience, and it attaches to male bodies, not to male self-conceptions. Male puberty is a performance-enhancing event with no antidote.
